explanation: The OK hand sign isn't offensive in China, but it isn't purely an 'approval' gesture either: the same thumb-and-finger ring shape is also one of the ways to represent the number three in Chinese hand-counting gestures. In practice this means it's generally safe to use but can occasionally cause mild confusion rather than being read as a thumbs-up-style compliment.
local_tip: Use the OK sign for agreement or approval if you like, but don't be surprised if an older or rural person reads it as the number three rather than 'okay.'

also_check.note: The gesture is a well-known vulgar insult, comparable to an obscene gesture rather than a sign of approval.
The gesture can be read as a crude insult in some contexts, so it's best avoided.
It can be understood to mean 'zero' or 'worthless' rather than approval, depending on context.
